attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'until' antecedent and the firm 'will have little choice'. 'After-the-fact' fairly reflects his point that suits come only after harm. 'Little choice' is a judgment about practical necessity with no stated measure.

contract.note: The plain reading (practical dependence on reactive suits while the federal gap persists) is ordinary and fair. The result depends on how 'more comprehensive' and the effectiveness of alternatives are judged, and the speaker defined neither.

evidence.note: The June 2 EO shows a narrow, voluntary, cybersecurity-focused policy in June. This bears on the antecedent, not the outcome, and does not show the policy was unchanged through October.
The March 2026 legislative framework is only a proposal. It does not show enacted federal protections and does not bear on whether states had alternatives.
The Oct 23 Texas DTPA suit fits the predicted pattern. Under the contract, though, another lawsuit alone does not show that states had little effective alternative.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated. The packet does not show whether the federal-policy gap persisted on the dates of later enforcement. It also does not show whether effective preventive alternatives, such as state safeguard laws, were available. A further state lawsuit fits the predicted pattern but cannot settle the 'little choice' claim, so the evidence does not resolve it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: A faithful restatement that keeps 'appears', '(effectively)' and the selective/reactive judgment. The core is a universal causal maxim wrapped in an evaluative description of the June 12 action.

contract.note: Correctly declines to score. 'Thrive' has no measure or period, and 'appears arbitrary' is an evaluative judgment. Supplying a metric would rewrite the claim.

evidence.note: In this Anthropic disclosure, the company confirms it removed access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 under the June 12 directive. This confirms the event he describes, not the causal maxim.

reviews.rationale: The claim joins a universal maxim (no industry can thrive under an apparently arbitrary government) with evaluative judgments about the June 12 action. It has no measurable criterion for thriving and no period. The suspension itself is confirmed, but that cannot settle the claim, so it is not adjudicable.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'appears to have panicked' hedge and the 'essentially every' scope. The checkable parts are the Amazon report sequence, near-universal jailbreak susceptibility, and that the problem predates the incident. 'Naive' and 'panicked' are evaluative.

contract.note: The plain reading of 'essentially every' (almost all major deployed systems, with exceptions allowed, and a narrow bypass is enough) is ordinary and fair. Excluding 'panic' and 'naive' from scoring is appropriate.

evidence.note: Anthropic's disclosure says the June 12 directive followed government awareness of Amazon researchers' bypass of Fable 5. That supports the sequence, though it is a company account. The same disclosure says every model Anthropic tested could produce the same exploit demonstration.
A peer-reviewed study (Feb 2026) reports about 97% jailbreak success against nine widely used models. This supports broad contemporary vulnerability, though not every deployed safeguard stack.
Prior research (2024, revised 2025) shows jailbreaks across GPT, Claude, Llama and other families. This supports that the problem is not new.

Anthropic's strongest classifiers resisted universal jailbreaks but still showed a high-risk vulnerability. This limits a 'universal jailbreak' reading but does not contradict narrow-bypass susceptibility.

reviews.rationale: Anthropic's account confirms the Amazon-report sequence. Peer-reviewed and earlier research shows widespread jailbreak susceptibility across major model families since at least 2024. Even heavily defended systems (Fable 5's safeguards, Anthropic's classifiers) had narrow bypasses. The e4 counterevidence only rules out universal jailbreaks, which the contract does not require. Coverage is not exhaustive, but under the loose 'essentially every' the checkable parts hold.
